text.p: Aston Villa goalkeeper Mark Bosnich, charged with misconduct by the English F.A. for making a Nazi salute during a match, received a character reference on Wednesday from soccer chiefs in his native Australia.
In a letter faxed to the F.A's London headquarters, Soccer Australia chairman David Hill described Bosnich as "an outstanding ambassador" for the sport in his homeland.

"Soccer Australia is proud of Mark's achievements and public profile," Hill wrote of Bosnich, who could also face criminal charges over the incident during a Premier League match at White Hart Lane on Saturday.
"His efforts on and off the field have only brought good upon his sport and he has gone out of his way to help further the cause of football in Australia."
Bosnich, whose actions incensed Tottenham fans, many of whom are Jewish, is Australia's first-choice goalkeeper and played in their unsuccessful 1994 World Cup qualifying campaign.
"While Soccer Australia would never condone Mark's actions in this matter, we do note his total, unequivocal retraction and expect that his action will not be repeated," Hill said.
Bosnich, whose family is of Croatian descent, has publicly apologised for his gesture, saying it was an attempt at comical mimicry.
Before the incident, Bosnich was baited by home fans about an incident 18 months ago when he knocked Tottenham's striker at the time, German Juergen Klinsmann, unconscious in a rash challenge.
Bosnich also received support from Sydney Morning Herald soccer writer Michael Cockerill, who described him as the Paul Gascoigne of Australian soccer.
"He is a constant ball of energy, always fidgeting, always talking. Loves a practical joke, savours being the centre of attention," Cockerill wrote.
Cockerill also drew attention to Bosnich's close friendship with fellow Australian international Milan Blagojevic, who is of Serbian origin.
"(It is a) friendship Bosnich values even more since the unfortunate events in former Yugoslavia. A racist? I think not?" he added.
